speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: asked the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (a) what are the factors that the Ministry considers before deciding to outsource the hawker centre management from NEA to private companies; and (b) whether the Ministry has oversight of the general contract framework or pricing models that the private management companies impose on their tenants.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: asked the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (a) what are the different types of new hawker centre models available today; (b) of all the current hawker centres, how many of them are under these new models of management; and (c) whether there is a timeline for measuring the effectiveness of each model when the new hawker centre models are being tested.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: asked the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (a) what challenges do hawkers face under the social enterprise hawker centres initiative; (b) what kind of pricing model should hawkers and patrons expect under this initiative; and (c) how is the Ministry addressing the unhappiness resulting from this initiative.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: asked the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (a) whether the total cost of running a hawker stall under the new social enterprise-run hawker centres model has been significantly higher than that of the NEA-run model; (b) whether the new model has helped serve the policy intent of providing affordable food and sustaining hawker culinary skills and trade; and (c) whether the contractual terms and requirements imposed by the operators of the new model on the hawkers are reasonable and fair.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: asked the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (a) whether the Ministry can stop further outsourcing of hawker centres to private operators; (b) whether the Ministry conducts an oversight of the contract terms between the management and tenants of outsourced hawker centres; and (c) what is the Ministry doing to resolve the many issues arising from its decision to outsource hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: asked the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (a) what are the key success factors that can be attributed to NEA-managed hawker centres in bringing affordable and good food to the public; and (b) what are the challenges in replicating the successful NEA-managed hawker centres to new hawker centres operated by social enterprises.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: asked the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (a) what are the cost components of running the existing hawker centres and markets; (b) whether there is a subsidy or grant given to each hawker or market stall and, if so, what is the subsidy; and (c) whether the same subsidy or grant is extended to social enterprise operators.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: asked the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (a) what has been the success rate of tray returns since the programme was launched; and (b) whether there is a need to redesign the tray return collection points through enhancement of the washing area for patrons to return direct to the washing area-cum-collection point for better efficiency and reduce bird-related hygiene issues.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: asked the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources whether hawker centre stall rental rates can be delinked from private market rental rates, including privately-owned HDB coffee shops, and free market bidding rates.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: asked the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (a) what measures are in place for the Ministry to take action against private operators of hawker centres who do not abide by the terms of the operating contract; and (b) what action can be taken against private operators of hawker centres whose actions or lack thereof lead to reputational damage for the Ministry, other Government agencies, hawkers and other community stakeholders.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: asked the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources whether the Ministry has considered working with NHB's Our Hawker Culture travelling exhibition to better grasp public opinion and tap new ideas on what Singaporeans expect of our hawker centres beyond providing affordable food.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: asked the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources where food supply is required at complexes that are open 24 hours, whether the Ministry has considered more strategic use of vending machines that provide hot food in place of mandating that hawker stalls remain open.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Minister, do you want to cover the rest of the questions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I will speak on why we embarked on the Socially-conscious Enterprise Hawker Centre (SEHC) model, how we select operators, and share our views on how the SEHCs are performing.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Senior Minister of State Amy Khor will elaborate further on our efforts to refine the SEHC model and better support our hawkers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Hawker centres are an integral part of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They are our community dining rooms – well-loved by Singaporeans from all walks of life.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They serve three key social objectives by providing: one, affordable food in a hygienic environment; two, a decent living for our local hawkers; and three, vibrant social spaces to bond our communities.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These are good objectives to achieve individually; but together, they compete against one another.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So, tradeoffs need to be made for an optimal outcome.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We were concerned about the lack of affordable dining-out options for Singaporeans at a time when there was a boom in coffee shops and food courts.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Natural market forces were pushing up rents at those private food and beverage (F&B) outlets and, consequently, food prices.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The public was concerned about the rising cost of living.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In response to widespread appeals by Singaporeans, we resumed building hawker centres to serve as a ballast to stabilise cooked food prices against the emerging dominance of coffee shops and food courts.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These will provide about 800 new hawker stalls at significant investments.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Government absorbs the building costs and subsidises their ongoing maintenance but does not recover such costs from stall rental.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We recognise, however, that just by building new hawker centres, we cannot automatically expect them to be viable and sustainable.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In the early 1970s, the Government started building hawker centres to resettle street hawkers, so as to improve hygiene and food safety standards.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Over time, they became our signature community dining rooms.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To this day, they enable us to preserve the important culture of eating out together, regardless of our status, rich or poor, young and old.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Over time, too, a good number of these first- and second-generation hawkers, who receive cheap subsidised rentals, only work short hours.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Residents, in turn, feedback that some existing centres do not fully cater to their dining needs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I was at Shunfu Mart Food Centre during a recent Ministerial Community Visit in Bishan East-Thomson Constituency.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The hawkers only open for breakfast and lunch; some even just for breakfast.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Residents do not have access to affordable food in the evening.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This situation reflects a need for the careful balancing act to look after the interests of both hawkers and the community.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But we also have to be fair to hawkers and safeguard their well-being.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our social and demographic landscape has changed significantly.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Many successful hawkers tell us that they hope their children will not follow in their footsteps.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The challenges of the trade deter many young Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have to transform and find ways to make the hawker trade sustainable, or we may end up with hawker centres without hawkers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The demographic profiles and needs of residents have also evolved, particularly in newer estates.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Patrons are more well-travelled and demand fresh concepts and wider food variety.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Hawker centres have to compete with coffee shops, food courts and other food outlets in the community.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Even the traditional model of dine-in meals has been disrupted by central kitchens and food delivery services.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We must help our hawkers meet these challenges, just like how we try to help our taxi drivers face the wave of challenges from disruptive competition like Uber and Grab.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To adapt to changing needs and circumstances, it is critical to find new operating models to sustain the hawker trade.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is similar to the role which the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) Fairprice has played in the supermarket landscape.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Over the years, NTUC Fairprice has been innovating and moderating prices of essential groceries, which has catalysed the transformation of the mom-and-pop grocery shops.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Over time, as customer profiles change, NTUC Fairprice continues to meet the needs of a wide spectrum of customers, by providing diverse product lines from affordable house brand options to premium brands.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Even NTUC Fairprice would not have been sustainable if they only provided affordable alternatives without the attraction of choice for their customers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is why we are trialling the SEHC model for our new hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have started at seven new hawker centres, out of more than 100 managed by the National Environment Agency (NEA).

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These SEHC operators bring new ideas and inject innovation that hawkers individually or the Government cannot.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are giving an opportunity to those with expertise and networks in the F&B industry to apply themselves to socially oriented purposes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For example, they are able to curate food stalls for quality and variety.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They are also able to bring in famous food recipes and are better placed to run hawker incubation programmes to help sustain the hawker trade.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They also innovate to improve footfall and enhance vibrancy of the centres through better marketing and place-making programmes, and not just leave it to chance.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As the single operator of each hawker centre, with F&B and management competencies, these SEHC operators can help our hawkers weather the competition from other F&B alternatives and adapt to technological disruptions better than the hawkers can individually.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In time to come, the better SEHCs will develop capabilities to support and sustain the hawker trade that we will appreciate.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To ensure that we select the right operators who do not profiteer, NEA has put in place safeguards through the tender and evaluation processes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: First, NEA favours operators with lower overall charges to stallholders.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: All new charges, including optional charges for value-added services, must be approved by NEA.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Third, a large part of the hawkers’ operating costs, like the Service and Conservancy Charges (S&CC) and table cleaning fees, are “pass-through” charges, which the operators do not benefit from.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As a reality check, we compare some of these costs with the alternatives like hiring additional hawker assistants, or the consequences of cheap sourcing low-quality workers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I am heartened by the recent public discussion on how existing NEA centres are run better than the SEHCs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is testimony that existing hawker centres under NEA management have done well over the years to meet the needs of their communities and the hawkers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But it is not enough to keep doing things the same way.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is why we have to continue with the SEHC model.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Several Members asked what makes a successful hawker centre.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I believe most of us have patronised our favourite stalls at popular hawker centres, such as at Tiong Bahru or Adam Road.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Many such existing centres are well-established in their communities.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They have anchor hawkers who draw customers from all over the island.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The new hawker centres do not enjoy this advantage and need time to build up a clientele.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: New hawker centres at Kampung Admiralty and Our Tampines Hub (OTH), situated at transport nodes and co-located with other public services or amenities, have enjoyed good business.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Higher business volume will help stallholders cope with costs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: On the whole, SEHCs have achieved good outcomes despite the short time they have started operations.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Foremost, food prices at SEHCs are affordable and comparable to existing centres.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These are generally lower than prices at surrounding coffee shops and food courts.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We cannot force hawkers to sell at cheap prices for all dishes at each stall.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This means that prices are not kept artificially low.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Instead, operators work with hawkers to offer a range of food offerings at different price points, so that there are both attractive options that residents are willing to pay for and, at the same time, affordable options when residents want that.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Some hawkers have also chosen to price their dishes low to attract more customers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For example, "Old Times" at the Kampung Admiralty Hawker Centre prices all dishes below $3.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Indeed, at each SEHC, there are close to 40 affordable options of various kinds of meals from 40 different stalls.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They have tapped on their networks of hawkers and have the expertise to conduct food tasting when letting out stalls.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They have also introduced interesting food options, such as prawn paste chicken rice and halal zi char, and new dining concepts.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This ensures a good variety of food options, which is not always a given in existing hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Even in popular hawker centres like Tekka, we can find rows of stalls offering similar food because NEA is required to award one vacant stall at a time based on tendered rentals to the highest bidder.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: NEA does not have a mechanism to curate an attractive collection of food options at each hawker centre, like in the case of the SEHC model.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Such an allocation system run by NEA would be complex to execute and be subject to potential audit issues.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: SEHCs are establishing themselves within their communities and serving the residents well.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Ci Yuan Hawker Centre recently passed its three-year mark.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: At Bukit Panjang Hawker Centre, the renewal rate is similarly high at 96%.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: SEHCs at Kampung Admiralty and OTH are also doing well with hardly any vacant stalls and a long waiting list of potential hawkers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is similar to NEA-managed hawker centres, where only 3% of cooked food stalls are vacant.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: SEHC operators have also kept their centres open during breakfast, lunch and dinner – a major request made by the public.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In contrast, some existing hawker centres focus on only one or two main meals a day, and some hawkers only work three to four days a week.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To ensure vibrancy, SEHC operators have also introduced creative initiatives to increase footfall, such as complimentary parking, lucky draw programmes and shuttle bus services for office workers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The SEHCs are leading a new model of clean and productive hawker centres, applying the best practices they have learnt in the private sector to overcome the constraints of labour shortage.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: All the SEHCs come with productivity initiatives, such as automated tray return systems (ATRS) and centralised dishwashing (CDW).

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Providing trained and properly supervised cleaners and a more hygienic environment have increased table turnover rates, benefiting both patrons and hawkers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The average tray return rates at SEHCs are much higher than those at our existing hawker centres because of the operators' efforts in implementing the ATRS.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It makes the jobs of our cleaners easier and alleviates manpower shortages that our hawkers face in looking for workers to wash dishes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: During my walkabout at Shunfu Mart Food Centre, I had noticed an economy bee hoon and nasi lemak stall which had a faded sign advertising to hire a stall assistant.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The hawker shared that her children were not interested in helping out at the stall and she had been unable to hire an assistant despite advertising for a long time.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: SEHCs have also managed to attract new entrants to sustain the hawker trade.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is an encouraging sign and can be attributed to various initiatives introduced by SEHC operators, for example, Timbre's Incubator Programme and OTMH's Train and Place Entrepreneurship Scheme nurture new hawkers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These efforts complement NEA's ongoing incubation stall programme (ISP), which has supported 12 aspiring hawkers to date.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Eight of them are still on the programme, while the rest had decided that they were either not suitable for the hawker trade or withdrew due to personal reasons.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In addition, the operators have introduced productivity measures, such as centralised dishwashing, which allow hawkers to focus on their cooking and reduce the amount of menial tasks they need to do.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Taken together, these initiatives reduce the physical burden of being a hawker and can go a long way to help sustain our hawker trade.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Nonetheless, the SEHCs will take time to establish themselves.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Ci Yuan Hawker Centre, the first SEHC, only started operating three years ago, with the latest at Pasir Ris opening in January.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Hawkers at these new centres need time to build up a clientele.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Many of the hawkers are also new to the trade and need time to experiment with their recipes and decide if this is the career for them.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The centres also need time to build up footfall.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The market mechanism is working, and the Government should not intervene unnecessarily in mandating low or no rental, which could otherwise affect fair competition.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We want to reward successful hawkers to sustain the trade and preserve our beloved hawker heritage.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is natural to have some level of churn as better hawkers replace those who are less suited for the trade.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Market forces would lead to a fair distribution of hawker stalls, which ultimately benefits residents.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is inappropriate for the Government to subsidise a hawker on the basis that business is poor.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This would be unfair to a better performing hawker who thrives on healthy competition.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It would also be unfair to other private sector food shop operators located in close vicinity to the centres.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The model must, therefore, ensure that rentals and costs are transparent and fair to hawkers, but cannot subsidise hawkers to the extent that it distorts the workings of the market.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In summary, despite implementation challenges, the SEHC model is generally sound.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Food prices are kept affordable with a good variety of high-quality options, and the majority of hawkers are doing well at the SEHCs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As with any trials and experiments, we cannot always get it right the first time.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I ask Members to give the model time to adapt, adjust and optimise the outcomes we seek to achieve: first, the availability of affordable food options that do not deny respectable earnings for our hawkers and, at the same time, moderate the free market F&B alternatives; second, a decent living for our local hawkers that is sustainable even while providing affordable options; and third, to preserve our hawker centres, where we are proud of our unique vibrant social spaces as community dining rooms where everyone goes to, where affordable food is also good food.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Senior Minister of State Amy Khor will take the rest of the questions and then we will take the supplementary questions.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Please let us know which questions you are taking.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In fact, I would like to take this opportunity to thank members of the public for the many views, discussions and suggestions that they have put forward.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We appreciate such views and feedback to help us to improve to better serve our hawkers and Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I will speak on our efforts to better support our hawkers and look after their well-being.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As a regulator, NEA must strike a balance between serving the public well, and ensuring the well-being of hawkers, while working to achieve the social objectives of our hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Residents should have access to affordable food in a clean setting for all three meals.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: At the same time, hawkers must be able to make a decent living, under fair tenancy terms and conditions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As with any trial, it is difficult to get the SEHC model right from the start, especially since we have not built new hawker centres for almost 30 years.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Let the market work; and when we get feedback, or issues are raised, we will move to address them swiftly and decisively, as we have done in the past month or so.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are not done with the stock-take of the model and will continue to refine it to better serve Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I will outline three areas of improvements which we have made and will continue to focus on.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: First, we will better support stallholders to manage costs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It is also shown through studies by the Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) that hawkers generally price food according to what the market can bear.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is influenced by competition in the vicinity and the demographic profile of customers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Hence, rentals do not directly affect food prices.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Nonetheless, for both our existing hawker centres and our new SEHCs or new centres, we have put in place measures to ensure that rentals are fair and not speculative.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For existing centres, we have removed the reserve rent and disallowed subletting and assignment.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For new centres, we have, in our tender evaluation, favoured tenderers who offer lower total rental and operating costs, and prohibit any increases in rentals or operating costs for the duration of the tenancy, as one of our priorities is to safeguard the interests of our hawkers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The median rental of stalls in comparable existing hawker centres is $1,700 per month, which is comparable to those of the new centres after accounting for the larger stall size, better-designed stalls and amenities at the new centres and, in some cases, the co-location of the new centres with residential properties as well as other amenities.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Stall sizes at our new centres of between 10 square metres (sqm) and 21 sqm are much larger than existing centres, which are between five sqm and 13 sqm.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is in line with rentals of non-subsidised stalls at our comparable existing centres, which range from $640 to $3,900 a month.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our hawker centre rentals, specifically those at SEHCs, are not linked to the rentals of surrounding coffee shops and food courts.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In fact, they are nowhere near the rentals at these private F&B outlets, which can range from $4,000 to $13,000 a month, before other operating costs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will continue to monitor and ensure that stall rentals in our new centres are reasonable to enable hawkers to make a decent living.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As for existing hawker centres, no stallholders are paying astronomical rentals.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The recent $10,000 bid was an outlier, and the bidder did not even commence operations.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Besides rentals, the operating costs at the SEHCs and existing centres are comparable, too.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, S&CC at the new centres are between $110 and $350 a month, within the range of $130 to $450 a month at our existing centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Similarly, table-cleaning fees at the SEHCs are between $300 and $550 a month, again, within the range of $200 to $830 a month at our existing centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Operating costs payable by hawkers at existing centres also frequently do not take into account the costs for dishwashing.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: At the majority of our existing centres, without centralised dishwashing (CDW), stallholders may have to hire dishwashers which could cost up to $1,500 a month, which is much higher than the average CDW charges.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Moreover, these hawkers often have difficulties hiring and retaining such hawker assistants, as my Minister has said earlier, too.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With the grant extension, stallholders at our new centres will enjoy 50% reduction in their CDW costs for the first year and 30% for the second year.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Currently, these grants are only available to hawkers at our existing centres under the PHC format.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: However, after a few years of operations with the new centres, we recognise that hawkers at the new centres may also need some support in transition as they need time to build up their clientele.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These productivity solutions, such as CDW and automated tray return systems (ATRS), are necessary to alleviate our tight manpower situation and help hawkers solve problems like staff shortage.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The average tray return rates of our SEHCs are far higher, at about 58%, than those at our existing hawker centres which are at about 25%.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: First and foremost, patrons should form the habit of returning their trays with the crockery after eating.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: A high tray return rate will directly benefit both patrons as well as hawkers as it will lead to a faster turnover of tables, keep the birds away and lead to a cleaner environment that helps attract patrons.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It will also ease the workload of our cleaners so that the cleaning companies do not have to keep increasing the number of cleaners, which will eventually lead to higher cleaning costs for the hawkers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Even if they want to increase the number of cleaners, they consistently face manpower shortage and issues with hiring.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Greater public education and close partnership between operators, hawkers and patrons are key.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Everyone must play their part towards ensuring a clean environment in our hawker centres to benefit both patrons and hawkers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In fact, most hawkers have welcomed the productivity initiatives implemented at our new hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Toh Swee Han, a 39-year-old hawker operating the "Mang Cheng Xiang Curry Rice" stall at OTH Hawker Centre, said that he was satisfied with CDW as it helped him reduce his cleaning costs significantly.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: He highlighted that CDW fees at OTH added up to only $700, before the productivity subsidy, while it would cost him about $3,000 to hire two assistants to cover the same workload.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: CDW also saves stallholders from paying additional water charges or managing an inventory of crockery and cutlery that has to be replaced due to wear and tear or loss.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Hygiene is better as they do not have to carry out dishwashing within the stall area.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We hope that this will alleviate the workload of our hawkers, especially the older hawkers, and make the trade more attractive to our younger hawkers by reducing menial work.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Following a Call-for-Collaboration (CFC) led by Enterprise Singapore (ESG), on behalf of NEA, HDB and JTC, NEA is partnering Network for Electronic Transfers (NETS) to provide interoperable e-payment solutions to our hawkers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Stallholders in SEHCs can take up the CFC e-payment solution for three years without paying transaction costs or terminal rental.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This will provide an additional option to SEHC operators to encourage stallholders to opt for e-payment.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The above subsidies will help to reduce the operating costs of our hawkers at the new centres in their initial years.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These will support them as they build up their customer base.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: There may be some other fees from value-added services that the SEHC operators provide, such as coin changing services, but these are optional.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Second, NEA will rebalance the soft touch regulatory approach towards SEHC operators and exercise greater oversight to safeguard hawkers' well-being.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA has reviewed some of the key contractual terms between the SEHC operators and stallholders.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Some of the terms were replicated from contracts the operators use in the other food establishments that they run.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In practice, operators have actually exercised flexibility with these terms.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA has taken in the feedback of hawkers and worked with the operators to make four key changes as an immediate priority.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Operators will be more flexible on stallholders' operating hours.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Operators will also engage stallholders who intend to open more than eight hours a day on how they intend to do so and whether they would have sufficient manpower, for example, through engaging stall assistants or joint operators.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As asked by a Member, operators can also decide if it is feasible to install food vending machines to meet meal requirements beyond operating hours, especially for small meals or snacks.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This would address concerns of some stallholders being locked into their tenancies.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They will also bear all legal fees related to the tenancy.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA will continue to engage both hawkers and operators to address concerns in other areas.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For instance, at OTH, the community had initially asked for a 24-hour hawker centre.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But as the demand from patrons has not materialised, both hawkers and the operator will recalibrate the arrangement.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA will also ask operators to communicate stall tenancy agreement terms in simple language to ensure that potential stallholders can understand them clearly before they commit to run the hawker stalls.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In our contractual review, we found that the operators, indeed, have shown flexibility.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, we have not observed any operators charging stallholders rentals for the remaining of their tenancy terms, in the case of premature termination.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The operators have also agreed to make changes to the terms I have just described, and to waive any legal fees for new tenancy contracts and renewals.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Whilst there is a need to rebalance our soft touch regulatory approach towards our SEHC operators, we recognise, as I have said, that they have shown flexibility through the contract review process, and are making changes to some of their terms and practices.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They have also shown innovation and creativity in implementing measures to drive footfall to the centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These include family carnivals and loyalty programmes, which offer discounts and other promotions to build up a pool of repeat patrons.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These safeguards are part of our efforts to manage and reduce the risks of profiteering.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We stand ready to act decisively should there be any mismanagement by the SEHC operators.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As part of our ongoing stocktake, NEA will look at the selection criteria for operators, what to leave to market forces and whether any other safeguards should be prescribed.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Third, all SEHC operators have set up structured feedback channels for their hawkers and have had at least one meeting.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They will continue to engage their hawkers regularly and address concerns together and quickly.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA officers will be present at these meetings.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I am hopeful that such structured and regular meetings will help encourage communication, resolve day-to-day issues and also reduce misunderstandings.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I attended one of these meetings at Ci Yuan Hawker Centre.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The atmosphere was constructive and stallholders had positive experiences to share.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, Zhang Li Jun, a 29-year-old hawker who has been operating the "Teochew Satay Bee Hoon" stall since 2015, said that with the Hawkers' Feedback Group, operators could proactively seek hawkers’ views on various matters relating to the hawker centre and stalls, and also work together on ideas to help the centre do better.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I had a fruitful dialogue recently with HC3.0 committee members, hawkers and food advocates passionate about preserving our hawker culture.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The participants contributed many ideas and we have agreed to set up a ground-up workgroup, comprising hawkers and other experts, to look at how to support new entrants to the hawker trade and sustain our hawker culture.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Many of the new centres are doing well.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: When I visited Kampung Admiralty Hawker Centre recently, the place was crowded and many patrons shared with me that they were happy with the wide selection of hawker food at affordable prices.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: One patron even told me about the $2.60 mee siam sold by "The House 22".

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Similarly, I met a group of ladies who frequent the OTH Hawker Centre.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They excitedly told me how happy they were with the many tasty hawker fare offered there, such as laksa by "Social Bite", and "Chicken Rice @ OTH".

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In fact, the father of Mr Kiang, who runs "Chicken Rice @ OTH", was among the pioneer batch of chefs who developed the famous Chatterbox chicken rice at Mandarin Hotel.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, I share with you this little secret, which means that the next time I go, it will be a longer queue.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But for those centres which are not doing so well, we are working with the operators and stallholders to increase footfall, improve business and serve their patrons better.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: What they need now is our support, not speculation and negative publicity that will keep patrons away and cause stallholders more hardship.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The latest efforts to discuss and resolve issues through regular dialogue is the right way to go.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In summary, we will continue to make adjustments and recalibrate the SEHC model to ensure that it continues to achieve the key social outcomes of our hawker centres, which are: to provide affordable food in a clean environment, allow our hawkers to make a decent living and build communities.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will seek and listen to feedback from hawkers and patrons and continue with our stocktake to further improve the model.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It is a community-based effort involving many stakeholders, including our hawkers, to sustain the hawker trade.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The UNESCO nomination will be an important recognition of our hawkers, as we let the world know about our local food and multicultural heritage.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As of 18 November, we have received 133,000 pledges online.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I urge Members and all Singaporeans who have yet to pledge to do so on the Our SG Heritage website.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I am heartened by the passionate discussions and support for hawker food and our hawkers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To sustain the hawker trade and preserve our hawker culture, I urge everyone to patronise our hawker stalls and support them.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I wonder if all Members in this House have visited our new hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: If you have not, I urge you to show your support by visiting and patronising them with your families and friends.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, a few more secrets, including some of my favourites, such as delicious min jiang kueh by “Munchi” at Yishun Park Hawker Centre, chendol from the dessert stall at Ci Yuan Hawker Centre run by a young hawkerpreneur, and zi char from “Jian Fa BBQ Seafood” at OTH Hawker Centre, just to name a few.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Parents should bring their children to our hawker centres to appreciate our hawker culture and heritage food.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Deputy Speaker, I would like to thank the Minister and the Senior Minister of State for their very elaborate response.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I think many Singaporeans and myself really enjoy all the hawker food and we are supportive of the idea, including the need to try new models for what is relevant for our time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But for the fact that because the term is called "social enterprise", it needs to clearly demonstrate that there is this element of social benefits, whether it is for the hawkers themselves or even for the consumers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I have two clarifications that I would like to ask the Minister or the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State elaborate more on what are these social benefits?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, it would be a direct benefit to the hawkers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, I was one of those who lobbied very hard to have a hawker centre in Yishun.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But many of us would like to see the hawker centres that are run by NEA that provide good and cheap food.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I know that the Minister and Senior Minister of State have explained about the social enterprise hawker centres.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But a lot of residents are asking what is the definition of "social enterprise".

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We do not see voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) who come in, but we see those social enterprises that are set up by big companies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The second question: does this translate into lower cooked food prices?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How do you ensure that economic meals that are available at the hawker centres are available all the time?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Because residents have told me that they were very often told "卖 完 了", or sold out.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If they want to buy the economic meals, the answer is, "卖 完 了".

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The third question: what I understand is that hawkers are managed by social enterprise hawker centre companies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Then, NEA staff oversee the social enterprise company.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What my residents have been asking is: why can we not take away all these layers?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Why can NEA itself not run the hawker centre, build up its own internal capability?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is something that many residents hope to see; they would like to see the old type of the hawker centres that offer good food at cheap prices, rather than giving us a hawker centre that is very beautiful but then, most of the time, the food is more expensive than at the coffee shops.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, I think the Minister did not answer my Question No 4 on the Incubation Stall Programme.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I think there is such a programme and I would like to know how many have been under this programme and whether they continued beyond the incubation period and, if they do not continue, what are the reasons?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Could Members who are asking supplementary questions direct them to a specific Minister?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Member has raised five questions in total, I think.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: First of all, this SEHC that the media has been using is a bit of a misnomer.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, what we are saying is, operators who tender for these hawker centres and run them, there must be a social mission.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, a social enterprise could be one of the operators or interested party to tender for the hawker centres, but not necessarily must be a social enterprise.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: What we have done is that within the tender conditions, we have ensured that there is a social mission.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As I have said earlier, the Minister had also said, there are various safeguards that we have put in place in the tender conditions to ensure that we need the social objectives of the hawker centres that we started building again in the first place.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And that is to ensure that we have affordable food options of a good variety in a clean environment, ensure that our hawkers can make a decent living and, of course, preserve our hawker culture and ensure the vibrancy of our hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have said a number of times what these are.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: A good example of a socially-conscious operator would be NTUC First Campus (NFC), which is part of NTUC and is a cooperative.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In selecting SEHCs, we also look out for how we can harness their expertise, which is actually the recommendation from the Hawker Centre Public Consultation Panel that we try and leverage the experience of these operators in F&B and in business management, in order to be able to put in place various initiatives and ideas to ensure and enhance the vibrancy of the hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In relation to that, the Member had a question about why not let NEA continue to run hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Minister had elaborated in detail some of the reasons why we need to look at new management model for our new hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The reasons are because there are inherent challenges in the hawker trade: ageing profile of our hawkers, where our existing hawkers' age profile is 60 years, which means that within 10 years' time, one third would retire if we do not attract new hawkers into the trade.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, it is renewal, manpower constraints, as well as the evolving needs and tastes of patrons; how do you ensure that what you offer meets the needs and demands of patrons?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Also, in existing hawker centres, as the Minister had elaborated, our existing hawker centres have been around for years; they are already established.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Many of them have anchor hawkers who are able to pull in the crowds.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But on the other hand, you would also note that many existing hawker centres, when you go, you are sometimes not sure whether the stall is open.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Only 35% of our hawkers in existing hawker centres open for three meals.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Most of them for one or two meals; some only work three to four days.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, does this then meet the needs of our community, especially the newer communities where there are many dual-income families and they need to access food through the day and through the week for three meals?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These are some of the challenges and, therefore, we looked at how we can try out and pilot new management models in order to overcome these challenges and to meet our social objectives.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: There are, of course, teething issues, and we are committed to looking at how we can recalibrate, make adjustments and improve the model, even as we look to implementing it for our new hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Economical meals – how come they are not available?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It depends on which point in time of the day you go to the stalls.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Basically, the majority of the SEHC stalls do offer at least one affordable option.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But let me say that we only ask that they offer at least one affordable option and we are not asking them to artificially suppress the prices of all their food options.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In fact, they can sell all the other food options at different price points, and that is really the concept of a community dining room, where people from all walks of life can come together, share a table and enjoy a meal at different price points.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And that will ensure that they will be able to make a decent livelihood.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Whichever hawker centre does not have enough of those economical meals, we can talk about it and we can talk to the operators.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I have been to many of them and they do offer affordable options, and these are good options.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Regarding the question on incubation stalls, we have launched an Incubation Stall Programme last year, just about over a year ago.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: When we started, we identified 13 stalls that we pre-fitted and we offered these to aspiring new hawkers who are not sure if they are interested to join the trade; they are passionate but they are not sure if they can make it.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It is pre-fitted, so we reduce the initial capital cost.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So far, we have received some 40 applications.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have increased the number of incubation stalls to 15.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In fact, they have actually been relatively successful.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But we also need to note that whatever model that we may adopt, there will always be challenges even as there may be benefits and, therefore, we need to give it time to settle down.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We implemented it only about three years ago.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In fact, the last one, Pasir Ris Hawker Centre, was just opened this year.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, it is really in its infancy; it is still evolving.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We had set it up with the intention that we will continue to monitor, evaluate, refine and improve the model.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But having said that, the SEHCs, at the present moment, have actually resulted in many positive outcomes for both patrons as well as hawkers and we do not want to undo those achievements.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Therefore, we will see how we can better calibrate and make adjustments to the model.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But as I have said, we are open to any model because the idea really is to benefit patrons, Singaporeans and hawkers.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I am going to ask Assoc Prof Walter Theseira, then Gan Thiam Poh and Melvin Yong.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: My question is: if hawkers are self-employed, then how can they be compelled by social enterprises or by the Government to work certain hours or to meet other conditions of work?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The problem seems to be that we are expecting the hawkers to bear some of the burdens of being an employee, but without the benefits of a guaranteed and stable income, for example.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They are required to open only five days, eight hours a day.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They enter into an agreement with the operators to operate a hawker stall subject to, of course, various conditions that they are agreeable to, and these are some of the conditions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The reason why you have to implement some minimum operating hours as well as minimum number of days, really, is because we want to make sure that the hawker centres are able to provide three meals – breakfast, lunch and dinner, throughout the day, and throughout the week – in order to ensure the vibrancy of the hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The hawker centres are built to serve the community, and one of the needs of the community, as I have said, especially in newer housing estates, is to have access to these food options for the three key meals.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: If you do not agree to such operating hours, then it would come back to the same thing that in some existing hawker centres, when you go there, they are closed or they are open for only half a day and it does not serve the needs of the community.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They actually enter into the agreement voluntarily and knowingly.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Senior Minister of State, I think my question has yet to get an answer, that is, cost structure between the subsidised and non-subsidised stalls, one by NEA and one by another model.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, there is already an implicit Government subsidy for both.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The cost structure for both existing centres' non-subsidised stalls and new centres, really, is quite similar.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Earlier on in my reply, I already gave a comparison in terms of rentals, that, basically, they are quite comparable and in line, taking into account the differences in age, stall size and so on of the hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In terms of operating costs, it is also quite similar, and I have also given Members a comparison.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: There will be costs in terms of service and conservancy charges, table cleaning.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I believe that the Senior Minister of State said that the higher end of the hawker stall rental range is around $13,000.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At about $3.00 or $3.50 a plate, the hawker will need to sell at least 3,000 plates just to cover the rent.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If our hawker stalls are to serve the objective of keeping our food prices affordable, will the Ministry consider implementing a cap on the rental to better manage food prices?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even at half that rental, at $5,000, you will still need sell at least 1,500 to 2,000 plates a month just to cover the rental.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I did not say that the top-end rental at our hawker centres is $13,000.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: What I said was that the rental of our hawker centres, new hawker centres, is nowhere near to where the rentals are for food courts and coffee shops which range, based on our survey, from $4,000 to $13,000, net of operating cost.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are not asking them to sell everything at budget prices.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In fact, if you go to the hawker centres, there is a soup stall that I saw in Kampung Admiralty, the prices range from $2.80 to $14.00 because it is premium; maybe there are scallops and all that.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, would you ask the next question?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can I ask one more supplementary question, please?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Okay, I will allow one last supplementary question.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: The Senior Minister of State mentioned that 50% of the surplus from the social enterprise must be ploughed back to the hawker centres or hawkers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Actually, to Member Melvin's question about rental cap which I have forgotten to comment on, our existing hawker centres, the non-subsidised stalls, are actually let out by tender.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, there is already a range of rental indications, and, in fact, we have removed the reserve rent.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Therefore, even for our new hawker centres, when we evaluate the tenders, there are two things that we do.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: First, we get the professional valuers to assess what a reasonable market rent will be, and they actually make reference to the tendered rents of the existing hawker centres, and we also use that as a guide.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, we will continue to monitor rentals to ensure that they are fair and reasonable to our hawkers so that they can make a decent livelihood.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It has only been one to three years.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It just goes to show that just as new hawker centres need time to build up, to establish themselves, so do the operators.
